plan.contextChunk: This figure shows the two rotation operations on a binary search tree as a pair of small subtree drawings joined by dotted arrows. On the right, the upper node is a gray circle labeled x with a short stub edge rising to an unnamed parent; x's left edge ends at the Greek letter alpha, and its right edge descends to a second gray circle labeled y whose two edges end at beta and gamma. On the left stands the other configuration: y is now the upper node holding the parent stub, x is y's left child, and the edges terminate at alpha and beta below x and at gamma below y. Subtrees appear only as these labeled edges, without triangles. Between the drawings, an upper dotted arrow points leftward with "LEFT-ROTATE(T, x)" set above it, and a lower dotted arrow points rightward with "RIGHT-ROTATE(T, y)" set beneath it. Placing the before and after shapes side by side isolates what a rotation touches, the link joining x and y and which of them owns the middle subtree beta. The left-to-right order alpha, x, beta, y, gamma survives in both pictures, which is what makes the operation a legal local repair to the pointer structure.

interactionPlan.concept: A tree rotation is a constant-size pointer repair: it swaps the parent-child roles of x and y and re-hangs the middle subtree β, changing the tree's shape while preserving the inorder sequence α, x, β, y, γ.
elements: gray circle node x (upper node in the right-hand configuration)
gray circle node y (right child of x on the right; upper node on the left)
short stub edge rising from the upper node to an unnamed parent
subtree edge α (left child of x in both configurations)
subtree edge β (left child of y before rotation; right child of x after)
subtree edge γ (right child of y in both configurations)
upper dotted arrow pointing left, labeled 'LEFT-ROTATE(T, x)'
lower dotted arrow pointing right, labeled 'RIGHT-ROTATE(T, y)'
inorder sequence strip showing α, x, β, y, γ in order

interactions.label: Implement LEFT-ROTATE(T, x)

api.does: returns n's left child (α, β, γ leaves act as empty subtrees)
returns n's parent, or null if n is the root
makes c the left child of n — one of the ONLY ways to mutate
makes c the right child of n — one of the ONLY ways to mutate
sets n's parent pointer to p (no-op if n is an empty subtree)
makes n the tree root, reattaching the parent stub
draws a highlight ring and note on the named node for your own commentary

interactions.frame: the current tree (nodes x, y and subtree leaves α, β, γ plus the parent stub) with the node(s) and pointer(s) the op just touched highlighted in red

input.label: Initial tree
input.default: x is root; x.left = α, x.right = y; y.left = β, y.right = γ

interactions.sample_code:
y = right(x)
setRight(x, left(y))
setParent(left(y), x)
setParent(y, parent(x))
setRoot(y)
setLeft(y, x)
setParent(x, y)
mark("rotation complete")
interactions.buggy_code:
y = right(x)
setLeft(y, x)
setParent(x, y)
setRoot(y)
// BUG: β was never moved — setLeft(y, x) overwrote y's old left subtree, so β is lost
interactions.success_check: y is the root holding the parent stub, y.left = x, x.right = β, β.parent = x, and the inorder sequence is still α, x, β, y, γ

interactions.label: Inorder invariant
interactions.teaches: The left-to-right reading α, x, β, y, γ is identical before and after the rotation — rotation reshapes the tree without violating binary-search order, which is why it is a legal local repair

demo_steps.title: Before and after
demo_steps.narration: The two drawings show the same five elements in two shapes: LEFT-ROTATE(T, x) turns the right picture into the left, and RIGHT-ROTATE(T, y) undoes it. Only the x–y link and the owner of β change.

demo_steps.title: Write the rotation
demo_steps.narration: Complete leftRotate(x) using the pointer ops. Each assignment replays as one frame: watch β slide from y's left side to x's right side, then x drop below y and the parent stub move to y.

demo_steps.title: Check the invariant
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the inorder sequence: the strip α, x, β, y, γ reads identically in both shapes. The rotation moved pointers, never keys — that is exactly why it preserves the BST property.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A rotation touches only the link between x and y and the middle subtree β — a constant number of pointer writes — yet preserves the inorder sequence, making it a safe local fix for balance.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Two small tree drawings side by side, joined by dotted arrows as in the textbook figure. Right-hand tree: x on top with a short parent stub, α as left leaf, y as right child with leaves β and γ. Left-hand tree: y on top with the stub, x as left child with leaves α and β, γ as y's right leaf. Nodes are light-gray filled circles with italic serif labels; subtree leaves are plain Greek letters at the ends of edges (no triangles). Between the trees, an upper dotted arrow points left under the label 'LEFT-ROTATE(T, x)' and a lower dotted arrow points right above 'RIGHT-ROTATE(T, y)'. During code replay, show one live tree (starting from the right-hand configuration) and highlight each pointer as it is reassigned; the final frame should match the left-hand drawing. In inorder mode, replace the arrows region with a horizontal strip α – x – β – y – γ.

authoredContext: The search-tree operations TREE-INSERT and TREE-DELETE, when run on a redblack tree with n keys, take O.lg n/ time. Because they modify the tree, the result may violate the red-black properties enumerated in Section 13.1. To restore these properties, we must change the colors of some of the nodes in the tree and also change the pointer structure. We change the pointer structure through rotation, which is a local operation in a search tree that preserves the binary-search-tree property. Figure 13.2 shows the two kinds of rotations: left rotations and right rotations. When we do a left rotation on a node x, we assume that its right child y is not T:nil; x may be any node in the tree whose right child is not T:nil. The left rotation “pivots” around the link from x to y. It makes y the new root of the subtree, with x as y’s left child and y’s left child as x’s right child.

discrepancies: The trees and arrows are drawn noticeably smaller relative to the canvas than in the source, with much wider horizontal separation between the two trees, so the figure reads as more sparse than the compact source layout

The upper and lower dotted arrows in the source are long, bold dotted lines with filled triangular arrowheads spanning most of the gap; the generated arrows are shorter, thinner dashed lines that stop well short of the trees
Node labels (x, y) and subtree labels (α, β, γ) are rendered in a smaller italic size relative to the nodes than in the source, reducing the bold typographic emphasis of the original
evaluation.notes: Both tree configurations, the bidirectional dotted arrows, and the LEFT/RIGHT-ROTATE labels faithfully reproduce the CLRS rotation figure, and the executable pseudocode workbench with step replay and inorder-invariant demo is a strong pedagogical addition; only the sparser proportions and lighter arrow styling detract from visual fidelity.
action_items: Enlarge the trees (node radius, spacing, and label font sizes) and bring the two trees closer together so the figure fills the canvas with proportions closer to the source.
Thicken the dotted arrows and extend them nearer to the tree edges so they visually connect the two configurations as in the original.
Increase the italic Greek/letter label sizes on nodes and subtrees to match the source's prominent typography.

feedback.rationale: Concept and interactivity are at 5/5 with no failure modes; the remaining issues are minor visual polish (proportions, arrow weight, label size) in an already strong figure, so further iteration offers diminishing returns.
